
=================================================================
#40 Gi (起)  (645 Autumn)
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: surabol · tone: envoy intrigue into chamber drama
Logline: Bidam takes the Council’s first chair and keeps his hand down alone against the queen’s cousin. The queen falls, the gate shuts, and on the first day the black headbands go up on the Radiance wall.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The Harmony Council has one rule. Nothing moves unless the circle closes. Everyone agrees, or nobody goes home.
[1] ── SCENE: The Harmony Council ──
[2] ¶ This winter the first chair has a new occupant. Old Supum is thanked for his years and sent home, and the queen gives his seat to the one councillor who has never once told her what she wanted to hear.
[3] [CARD Bidam — High Councillor of Silla: First chair of the Harmony Council. Every vote now passes through his hands.]
[4] ¶ Under him sit the others, Yushin among them. They still decide only by unanimity. It’s the only way this council selects anything.
[5] ¶ Then the room turns to the question everyone has been circling: when Her Majesty fails, who next. The Sacred Bone has thinned to one cousin. Someone says the name **Princess Seungman** the way you set a cup down that you expect everyone to drink from. She is forty-five, kind, careful with servants, and has never once surprised anybody.
[6] ¶ One by one the hands go up. In a unanimous council a raised hand is a kind of weather — once it starts, it finishes. **Yushin**’s hand is among them. He has served one queen; he will serve her cousin.
[7] ¶ Only one hand stays down.
[8] ¶ Five pieces go to the yes side of the cup. Bidam’s piece stays on the no side.
[9] [DIAGRAM harmony-council:veto Harmony Veto · 화백 거부 — Five assent, Bidam’s hand stays down. The cousin’s name cannot pass.]
[10] Kim Murim: Bidam. This is the initial vote. / Five are up. What is there to deliberate. / We cannot even open the final vote. / You locked the door.
[11] Kim Suljong: One hand down and this room is finished. / You know that, and you still put it down?
[12] Bidam: I object.
[13] ¶ The room does the small silence of men who have already counted themselves finished. Unanimity has failed. The name cannot pass. Someone laughs once, short, the laugh you make when the host spoils his own dinner.
[14] Alchun: Bidam… alone? / It is Princess Seungman.
[15] Bidam: Princess Seungman is not as clear-sighted as Her Majesty. / We cannot hand the country over for Sacred Bone alone. / Thirteen years ago, when I stood for Princess Dukman, it was because she was the cleverest. / Now you ask me to throw that measure away.
[16] Kim Yushin: Bidam. Come on. / Same blood. Same house. / Thirteen years ago you put her cousin on that chair yourself.
[17] Bidam: Which is exactly why I’m saying no, you Gaya ox. / Don’t give me that face. A hundred and eight to a hundred and eight, remember? Neither of us ever got to be right for long. / A country is not a scoreboard. / And on a night when Lord Chunchu’s eyes turn toward Chang’an, you want another soft Sacred Bone on that chair? Then who sells this country?
[18] ¶ Yushin does not answer the count. Something in his face closes that has been open since they were boys on the yard. The Council adjourns with no successor named.
[19] ¶ In the emptied hall the incense has burned down to a stub. Bidam has not left the table. His fist is still on the wood, the way his father’s was on the morning he walked him to the yard.
[20] Bidam: …Alone, Father. Just as you said.
[21] ▼ FLASHBACK 610 The higher teaching · 아비달마
    [21.0] ¶ Class 51’s first morning. Packed earth still dark. Bidam is sixteen. His father walks him as far as the yard gate and no further — Musan hall does not hover.
    [21.1] [CARD Son Sukwon: Bidam’s father. A man of few words, and he has saved them all for his son.]
    [21.2] Son Sukwon: Bidam… / Do you know the meaning of your name.
    [21.3] Bidam: Yes, father… / I was named after the Abhidharma, the higher teaching. It—
    [21.4] Son Sukwon: Yes… the higher teaching. / And as a young man, and as a Hwarang, your duty is to uphold that. / And remember this: / Even if no one else agrees with the truth… even if speaking it out loud causes others to defame and mock you… / You must always walk toward the truth, in isolation if you must. There is no other way. / You may have heard the saying: upon victory, a king; upon defeat, a traitor. / Son… I need you to be a man who would rather be a **righteous traitor** than an unrighteous king. / Bidam… I love you…! / Go make us proud, son…!
    [21.5] ¶ He does not name the Gaya-born boy who will share the class. He only ties Bidam’s headband once, tight, and lets the gate take him.
[21] ▲ end flashback
[22] ── SCENE: Princess Seungman ──
[23] ¶ Princess Seungman catches him at the palace gate. Word has reached her before he has.
[24] [CARD Queen Jinduk: The queen’s cousin, and the last of the Sacred Bone.]
[25] Queen Jinduk: Bidam…! What is this I hear? / Surely not…
[26] Bidam: You heard right, Princess. One hand. Mine.
[27] Queen Jinduk: She can barely sit up, Bidam. The physicians say a season. Less. / Couldn’t you let her have one quiet winter?
[28] Bidam: I gave her thirteen quiet winters. I put her on the chair. / She was chosen because she was the cleverest. Now the room wants the nearest. / Forgive me, Princess. You are kind. Kindness does not hold a pass.
[29] Queen Jinduk: …Then who holds it? You?
[30] ¶ He bows the full bow, the one owed to the Sacred Bone, and does not answer. Seungman watches him go the way you watch weather you can’t stop.
[31] ── SCENE: Alchun’s Door ──
[32] ¶ He starts counting who would come with him, and the first door he knocks on is Alchun’s.
[33] Bidam: The problem is these rotten ministers!
[34] Alchun: Oi. Enough of that ignorant talk. / The level of the ministers is the level of the country. / If the people were clear-sighted, the ministers would notice and do their jobs.
[35] Bidam: What are you talking about! / Do you look down on the people of this sacred country? / They have always—
[36] Alchun: Yes. I look down on them. So what? / If everything is this rotten and you lie there doing nothing, some of the blame is yours. / Why is it always the most ignorant in a country who shout loudest that it is the greatest…
[37] Alchun: …And use your head. If Princess Seungman doesn’t take the throne, who sits there? / There’s one more royal neck in Surabol. Chunchu’s.
[38] Bidam: Precisely.
[39] Alchun: Ah, he doesn’t want it. Told me so himself, over wine. / Laughed at the whole idea, he did.
[40] Bidam: Chunchu is the most cunning man in Samhan…! / Never — not for one moment — believe a word that comes out of that mouth…!
[41] ── SCENE: The Harbour ──
[42] ¶ Chunchu is sailing east to ask the islands for ships. Munhee packs for him. She has packed for every trip he’s ever taken. She will pack for one more. Nobody writes any of this down, which is why it needs saying.
[43] Munhee: How many months this time?
[44] King Muyeol: …I don’t know.
[45] Munhee: Then I will pack for more.
[46] ¶ At the harbour the wine merchant Haesang sees him off with advice nobody asked for.
[47] Haesang: If you reach the eastern islands, my lord, ask after their lacquer. / And if you ever reach Chang’an — ask after a woman who finishes the emperor’s sentences. Merchants hear weather early.
[48] ── SCENE: The Queen’s Chamber ──
[49] ¶ Bidam hears it from a harbour clerk, which is the worst way to hear anything. Chunchu has sailed east. The queen signed the order herself. Nobody asked the Council.
[50] ¶ He finds her in the small hall, not the throne room. She is sitting very straight, the way people sit when they no longer trust themselves to lie down.
[51] Bidam: …Why wasn’t this told to the Council? / Lord Chunchu isn’t even a member of the Council… he’s just… / …your nephew…
[52] Queen Sunduk: Lord Bidam… I-I need to lie down…
[53] ¶ She tries to stand and doesn’t finish. Bidam catches her before the floor does.
[54] Bidam: Y-Your Majesty! GUARDS! THE QUEEN IS DOWN!
[55] ¶ Physicians. Doors. By evening the palace has stopped answering questions.
[56] ── SCENE: The Eastern Court ──
[57] [MAP 645: ]
[58] ¶ Across the sea, Chunchu has no idea. The King of the East receives him politely, which is its own kind of answer.
[59] [CARD King Kōtoku: The King of the East. His politeness comes with a price list.]
[60] King Kōtoku: Baekje — the Land of the Heavenly Deer, Land of the Lord Buddha — is our ally. / With respect — I must refuse peace with the Divine Country.
[61] King Muyeol: Baekje is a country on its way to ruin…
[62] King Muyeol: Our sacred country has produced no end of talent, / and yet not one man the equal of Goryeo’s Gesomun.
[63] King Kōtoku: You… speak our language remarkably well.
[64] King Muyeol: Sun Tzu says the highest strategy is to win without fighting. / If Chunchu may add one word: if fight you must, the highest strategy is to fight by borrowing another’s hand. / Too many of Silla’s young men have already died…! / How am I to face their parents?
[65] ¶ He asks for troops. He asks twice.
[66] ❝QUOTE (Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 25, Emperor Kōtoku — Taika 3 (647)): Silla sent its high minister, the Daeachan Kim Chunchu, with others, escorting home the scholar Takamuko no Kuromaro and Nakatomi no Oshikuma; they presented a peacock and a parrot. Chunchu was kept as a hostage. Chunchu was handsome, and good at talk and laughter.❞
[67] The Eastern Scholar: Chunchu… do you truly mean to go begging to every country around you? / Even Yamato has heard of the Eternal General and the Sword of the Divine Country. Silla may not be the power it once was, but we have strength enough to fight Baekje and Goryeo ourselves.
[68] ── SCENE: That Night ──
[69] ¶ That night Bidam takes the old black headband out of the chest where he keeps it. There is still blood on it, gone brown with the years. Two seniors’ noses, the first morning on the yard.
[70] Bidam: …I offered this to that boy, back then. / Told him nobody would trouble him if he had it.
[71] Bidam: I did not know the one troubling him would turn out to be the country.
[72] Bidam: As young Hwarang, they told us we’d be the future of this nation… / to protect the Sacred Bone class… / Bullshit… / “Sacred Bone class”? You mean the two dying grandmas?
[73] ── SCENE: The Moon Palace ──
[74] ¶ Nine days later the gate of the Moon Palace is still shut. The guards have orders to open it for no one. No one, it turns out, includes the Harmony Council.
[75] Bidam: WE’RE THE HARMONY COUNCIL! WHY CAN’T WE ENTER THE PALACE?? / WHAT AUTHORITY DO YOU HAVE? / SHE’S DEAD, ISN’T SHE? / THE QUEEN IS DEAD, AND YOU’RE HIDING IT FROM THE PEOPLE!! / DID CHUNCHU ORDER THIS?
[76] ¶ The guards look at their spears. Chunchu is across the sea. His orders, apparently, are not.
[77] ── SCENE: Yumjong ──
[78] ¶ Bidam does not recruit with speeches, whatever the Council thinks of him. He recruits with tea and long silences, and the first man to drink the tea is **Yumjong**, a True Bone whom nobody has ever accused of anything, because nobody has ever noticed him.
[79] [CARD Yumjong: A quiet True Bone who drinks his tea slowly and listens fast.]
[80] Yumjong: The islands, now. Last summer it was the emperor’s war. / Your Lord Chunchu does get around.
[81] ▼ FLASHBACK 645 Thirty thousand · 삼만
    [81.0] ¶ Earlier that summer the emperor in Chang’an marched on Goguryeo himself. Chunchu talked the queen into lending him men. Silla did not have the men to lend. Baekje noticed.
    [81.1] Bidam: Thirty thousand of our sons, Lord Chunchu. For another man’s war.
    [81.2] King Muyeol: Not a gift, Bidam. A loan. / Empires keep their ledgers longer than kings keep their thrones.
    [81.3] Bidam: Leave your own field to plough another man’s, and it grows weeds by autumn. / Baekje is the weeds.
[81] ▲ end flashback
[82] Bidam: Chunchu wants absolute power…!
[83] Bidam: What’s the difference between the West and the East anyway? / In both nations, their emperors cannot be removed by a vote. / Their people live as slaves.
[84] Yumjong: And the Marshal?
[85] Bidam: Yushin stands where the Queen stands. He always has. / When she is gone he will stand where the next one stands, and he will call it loyalty, and he will even be right.
[86] Yumjong: He’s not even Silla, you know. / Gaya. His great-grandfather handed over Geumgwan with the keys still warm. The men in the outer works would like hearing that.
[87] ¶ Bidam’s beads stop. He has said the word to Yushin’s face a hundred times on the yard, and Yushin has laughed every time. He has never heard it said like this, by a man who means it as a door.
[88] Bidam: …Careful, Yumjong. / A word you shout at a man’s gate comes back to your own. Gaya.
[89] ¶ He says it once more, under his breath, as if testing the weight.
[90] Yumjong: So. How many men, Councillor?
[91] Bidam: A paddy is not planted in a morning, Yumjong. One shoot, and then the next, and then the water does the rest. / Enough for the Fortress of Radiance. By the time Her Majesty’s breath runs out.
[92] ¶ Bidam sets the cup down. Chunchu is across the sea. The queen is behind a shut gate. The Council has no one left to ask. So, for the first time in his life, Bidam decides something without a vote.
[93] ══ DAY: DAY 1 ══
[94] ¶ **Queen Sunduk** is in critical condition. The Eastern Palace smells of medicine and of a succession nobody has settled.
[95] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonder 1 — Queen Seondeok knows three things in advance; Ha & Mintz tr., p. 73 · Ilyeon, Lee Byong-do ed., p. 98): I shall die in such a year, on such a month and day. Bury me in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.❞
[96] ¶ Princess Seungman sits on the edge of the sickbed with a comb, because somebody has to do the Queen’s hair and the maids’ hands shake. They are cousins, five years apart, the last two Sacred Bone women in the world, and they have been doing each other’s hair since the younger one was tall enough to reach.
[97] Queen Jinduk: Hold still, unni. / …You’ve gone thin at the temple. When did that happen.
[98] Queen Sunduk: While you weren’t looking. That’s when everything happens. / Pin it high. If I’m going to the Thirty-Three Heavens I want to look taller than the gods.
[99] Queen Jinduk: Don’t. / Don’t talk about where you’re going like it’s the market.
[100] Queen Sunduk: …Seungman-ah. You’ll have to sit in it. / I’m sorry. It’s a hard chair. I’ll leave you a cushion.
[101] ¶ Seungman pins the binyeo high, exactly where the Queen asked, and does not answer, which is the only way she has ever won an argument with her.
[102] ── SCENE: The Fortress of Radiance ──
[103] ¶ Bidam and Yumjong raise men at the Fortress of Radiance. The slogan is old. They only give it a banner. Yumjong holds the outer muster. Bidam walks the rampart as if the stones owed him rent. Inside the palace, the stewards count the grain and arrive at ten days. Nobody says the number aloud. Everybody schedules by it. The rebels tie on black headbands, Bidam’s old colour from the yard, so they can tell their own from the palace blue. Bidam ties on the old one, brown stain and all.
[104] [battle]
[105] [PLACE radiance: Close enough to the palace to shout at it.]
[106] ¶ He carries the heavenly-horse sword in the dark. The robe eats the lamp. Only the ring pommel holds the light — a gold circle at the end of old-hall steel.
[107] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin (Bidam’s rebellion, 647); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2): Bidam and the others encamped at Myeonghwal Fortress; the royal army camped at the Moon Palace. Attack and defence lasted ten days without being broken.❞
[108] ¶ Before the banner goes up he lights a stick of incense on the rampart and waits for it to take, because a man raised on this soil’s sutras does not begin a thing without the smoke. His hand is steady. Under the sleeve the beads have not moved once since the muster began.
[109] ❝QUOTE (Dhammapada (法句經) ch. 9, The Twin Verses (雙要品), tr. Weiqinan & Zhu Jiangyan · T04n0210, p. 562a · Pali: Dhammapada 1, Yamakavagga) [Bidam]: Mind is the root of all things: mind is the master, mind sets them moving. If the heart thinks evil and then speaks it and does it, guilt and suffering follow of themselves, as the wheel rolls in the rut.❞
[110] Yumjong: Put it on the banner. ‘A woman cannot rule well.’ / The men in the outer works don’t march for councils. They’ll march for that.
[111] Bidam: I crowned a woman, Yumjong. I stood up in that room and did it.
[112] Yumjong: Then you know exactly what the slogan is worth.
[113] Bidam: …女主不能善理. The room said it the year she was crowned and pretended it was weather. / Put it up. Let them march for the weather. / We won’t storm the palace. We wait.
[114] Yumjong: For what?
[115] Bidam: Ten days of grain in there. On the tenth morning the gate opens from the inside. / The Council sits with every chair full, and the succession goes back to the room where it belongs.
[116] Yumjong: Open the Radiance gate. / High Councillor Bidam comes — today it is the banner, not courtesy.
[117] ── SCENE: Between the Camps ──
[118] ¶ Before noon **Alchun** is summoned twice — once by the Sword of Silla, once by the High Councillor with a banner — and he answers both.
[119] Alchun: Yushin… / Of course we all loved the princess as young Hwarang. She was a beautiful princess, and we were young men. / But those days are over now. / You need to judge what is best for the nation — and the nation demands that you not be blinded by your personal loyalties, and judge what is best for the divine nation.
[120] Alchun: Bidam… / You swore allegiance to the Hwarang, and the divine nation has vested you with the authority of the High Councillor — the highest office in the land. / For you to take up arms against the crown would be an act of highest treason.
[121] Alchun: I will not raise a blade against Bidam. / I will not raise a banner against Her Majesty. / Ask me again on the tenth day. I may still be a coward — but I will be a precise one.
[122] ¶ Neither man answers him in a way that would satisfy a clerk. Yushin stares at the eastern palace. Bidam smiles as if treason were a word invented by cowards. Alchun walks back to the space between the camps and eats alone.
[123] ── SCENE: Dusk on the Wall ──
[124] ¶ By dusk Yumjong’s men have found a word they like. They shout it across the field at the blue lines, the way boys throw stones at a dog to see if it bites. Gaya.
[125] ¶ On the rampart a young officer brings Bidam his rice. The black headband on him is an hour old. So is his nerve.
[126] A young rebel officer: Councillor— forgive me. / What is Gaya, anyway? My father says it was a kind of iron.
[127] Bidam: Your father isn’t wrong. / Six harbours down the southern river, selling iron to anyone with rice. Us. Baekje. The islands. Enemies included. / No one king. Six chiefs and a great deal of arguing. Rather like our Council, only richer.
[128] A young rebel officer: And they lost?
[129] Bidam: They were bought. One harbour at a time. / The Marshal’s great-grandfather drove the oldest one to Surabol in a cart and set his crown on our king’s floor.
[130] A young rebel officer: Then why does it still—
[131] Bidam: Sting? / Because they have a better story than we do. / Their first king came down out of the sky in a golden egg. His queen sailed in from the end of the world under a red sail. / We tell our beginnings at funerals. They tell theirs at weddings.
[132] ¶ Below the wall his horse, Bisamun, shifts in the lines. Across the field, under the blue banners, a man with Gaya eyes is not shouting back.
[133] ¶ **A sky that looks too long at a mountain. Six eggs. A red sail. Here is how Gaya began…!**

=================================================================
#41 Suro  (42)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: geumgwan · tone: founder fairy tale
Logline: Before there is a Gaya, there is a ridge, and a sky god who looks at it too long.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Before there is a Gaya, there is a ridge, and a sky god who looks at it too long.
[1] ¶ **Ibiga** keeps the sky the way other gods keep a hall — cloud is his body, the living world a map he does not usually read. Then he looks down.
[2] [CARD Ibiga: The sky god. Cloud is his body, and he does not usually look down.]
[3] ¶ On her mountain the Lady of the Right View is on watch. At first she is the ridge — jade stone, mist, a woman’s shape the mountain has not admitted yet. The mountain is a woman before it has a face. Then a face comes out of the stone. She is guarding the mountain as if it were a country. She does not look up. She does not need to. Then the sky occupies the path. Cloud comes down to the ridge.
[4] [CARD Lady of the Right View: The mountain goddess. The ridge was a woman before anyone noticed.]
[5] Ibiga: That ridge… / That woman. / I have flown this path a thousand times. Why is the mountain looking back.
[6] ¶ Love arrives as weather — sudden, unasked. He cannot keep the hour. He falls before he lands. The sky comes down to touch the mountain, and does not leave.
[7] Ibiga: Mountain. / Your shoulder… is warmer than cloud. / Your waist… steeper than cliff.
[8] Lady of the Right View: Why has heaven come down. / To look? / Or… to touch. / If to touch… kneel first.
[9] Ibiga: To touch. / I looked… and could not hold back. / The knees… already are.
[10] Lady of the Right View: Then closer. / Ridges do not keep guests long. / Tonight I will make an exception. / I will keep your mouth… at my throat.
[11] Ibiga: Your name… Right View. / The longer I look, the less rightful my thoughts become. / I want to put heaven… between your thighs.
[12] Lady of the Right View: Then stay wrongful. / Nights when heaven kneels on a mountain… are not so common. / Kneel. / All the way.
[13] ¶ Cloud covers the ridge. What happens under it is not for the song. By the time the cloud thins, neither of them is kneeling, and neither of them has let go.
[14] ¶ He holds her with one arm. The other is cloud. The ridge is still a mountain; the mountain is still a woman. She does not look up. She does not have to.
[15] ¶ By morning the ridge remembers two gods who would not let go. From that heat come eggs, and from the eggs, kings.
[16] ¶ Their eggs fall to earth on a hill called Guji, and wait for someone to sing.
[17] [CARD King Suro: King Suro. Born from a golden egg, and in no hurry to marry anyone local.]
[18] ── SCENE: Mount Guji ──
[19] ¶ On Earth, the people sing a song to call for a new king.
[20] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 2, Wonder 2 — King Suro / Turtle Song; Ha & Mintz tr., p. 158): Turtle, turtle — show your head. If you do not, we will roast and eat you.❞
[21] ¶ The people dig where the song tells them and find a box of six eggs, gold as the sun. Six babies hatch. The first one out is Suro. Each of the six founds a harbour kingdom:
[22] The Herald: …Eggs, you said?
[23] A villager: Six. In a box. From the sky.
[24] ¶ Nobody in Samhan finds this remarkable. Silla’s founder came out of an egg. Goguryeo’s founder came out of an egg. Here are six more. At some point one has to ask what the birds were doing.
[25] ¶ Gaya doesn’t have a crown. It has a league of iron harbours, six of them, give or take. No one king can lock the vote. Surabol would find that exhausting.
[26] [DIAGRAM gaya-league Gaya Confederacy · 가야 — Not one crown — a league of iron harbours.]
[27] [PLACE geumgwan: The harbour that sells iron to everyone, enemies included.]
[28] ── SCENE: The Red Sail ──
[29] ¶ **Queen Heo**, an Indian princess, becomes the first queen of Golden Gaya.
[30] [CARD Queen Heo: Heo Hwang-ok. She sailed farther than anyone in Samhan had heard of, and arrived dressed for it.]
[31] ¶ She arrives on a red-sailed ship at twenty-one — foreign, luminous, built like nowhere on this coast. The beach is only a door. The first time **Suro** falls in love is not on the sand.
[32] ¶ In the timber court of Golden Gaya she presents herself — no servant speaking for her, her own name, silk that does not belong to this hall. He is already on the dais. He meant to receive a princess. He receives a woman, and love hits him before protocol can stand up.
[33] ¶ Protocol is still trying to stand. He is already off the dais. He comes down with one arm — gold around violet, the same hold the sky used on the ridge, only this time the hall has columns and a floor.
[34] ¶ Servants had been sent to the ship. She refused them. So the court is where they meet — and the moment he sees her, speech leaves him like heat from an open kiln.
[35] Queen Heo: Have you come to fetch me… / or have you already begun to take me. / With your eyes. / Your mouth… looks dry.
[36] King Suro: … / ……You. / Your mouth…
[37] Queen Heo: Yes. / My mouth. / When the king looks at me like that… I get warmer. / Your hands… where do you mean to put them. / Even if you can’t speak — your hands know.
[38] King Suro: Your waist… / I mustn’t… / If I touch…
[39] Queen Heo: Then touch. / Since the king can’t choose… I’ll choose for you. / Here. / And here. / You’re shaking.
[40] King Suro: …Hungry… / I can’t… speak…
[41] Queen Heo: Then don’t speak. / If you’re hungry… take me first. / Slowly. / Not like a king — like a man.
[42] ¶ He makes a sound that is nowhere near a word, and she smiles as if it were the only answer she came across the sea for.
[43] ¶ On the hill she offers her silk trousers to the mountain spirit. He watches as if the rite were meant for him alone — jaw tight, hands useless at his sides.
[44] King Suro: …How will we know the mountain accepted it?
[45] Queen Heo: I can tell from the king’s eyes. / You look like someone who has already received.
[46] King Suro: …It is not I who received. / …I am going mad wanting to.
[47] Queen Heo: This country. / And by tonight… its king.
[48] ── SCENE: The Tent by the Water ──
[49] ¶ Two nights in a tent by the water before anyone may say marriage. By the second dusk he can barely keep his voice steady when she says his name — and she says it into his mouth so he has to swallow it.
[50] ¶ She turns so he can see the curve of her hip catching lamp, and he is kissing the throat he will marry before he has permission to call it a country.
[51] ¶ When he turns to the lamp she looks at the width of his back — muscle under purple-gold silk, a king’s body that the court never sees — and does not hide how that look sits on her mouth.
[52] Queen Heo: Slowly. / Your tongue — here. / The way you say my name. / The lower lip. / Below that. / More.
[53] King Suro: …At this rate I will learn the language. / Or I won’t. / I think I will fall apart first. / Inside you…
[54] Queen Heo: Then fall. / That way I have to put you back together every night. / With hands. / With mouth. / Until the king is a king again.
[55] ¶ The lamp burns low. She has taught him a dozen words since the dais, and in the dark she teaches him the rest without any — her hand on his wrist, showing him where, laughing when he is slow, then not laughing at all. She is twenty-one and crossed a sea with a stone pagoda in her ship’s hold to stop the waves; he is a king who hatched from an egg and has never once been told how. Neither of them is a god tonight. They are clumsy and greedy, and by the second hour they are good at it.
[56] King Suro: Say it— say it again— / In your Ayuta tongue— my name— / …I have forgotten what my own country is called—
[57] Queen Heo: My king— more— / Haa— my country has no word for this either— / Not yet— don’t go—
[58] ¶ The second night she is on top, violet silk off her shoulders and the gold tiger-pins still in her hair, because she refuses to take them out for a man who cannot yet say _good morning_ in her language. He loses his own words again. She keeps hers. When she comes apart she says something in the tongue of Ayuta that nobody on this coast will ever translate, and he decides it was his name.
[59] Queen Heo: My king’s— ah— / Stay— just like that—
[60] King Suro: …Wife. It is morning. / I cannot… take my hands away.
[61] Queen Heo: I know. / But I have not yet learned this country’s hours.
[62] King Suro: …The ministers are outside. / Before I go in… once more.
[63] Queen Heo: Once? / What a modest king.
[64] King Suro: I am not modest. / …I am only holding on. / Barely.
[65] Queen Heo: It does now. / I brought it with me — that sound, that night.
[66] ¶ They are married a hundred and fifty years — the record is firm about this and entirely untroubled by it — and have ten sons. She asks that two of them carry her name instead of his. He agrees without an argument, which in the whole of this history is the single strangest thing any king does.
[67] [WEDDING Queen Heo + King Suro]
[68] Queen Heo: My country is gone. Only the name is left.
[69] King Suro: Then we keep the name. I can always make another country.
[70] ¶ She dies at a hundred and fifty-seven. He follows ten years later and asks to be laid where he can see her hill.
[71] ¶ Her sons have her eyes, the colour of the far side of the sea. Gaya will marry into Silla and lose almost everything else. The eyes keep turning up anyway, a generation here and there, like a word nobody can quite translate.
[72] ══ DAY: DAY 2 ══
[73] ¶ Back on the Radiance road, the second morning comes up grey. Nine days of grain behind the palace gate. Bidam sends a runner across the field with a folded note. It says one word: tea.
[74] ¶ **Nine days of grain. One folded note. Will the Marshal of Silla come to tea with a traitor…?**

=================================================================
#42 Seung (承)  (647 January)
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: surabol · tone: political thriller — countdown
Logline: Five nights of tea between the camps, and a score still tied. On the fifth, Bidam asks the one question Yushin has never answered in Surabol.
=================================================================
[0] ══ DAY: DAY 2 ══
[1] ¶ Of course he comes. Yushin has never once refused Bidam a rematch. Between the camps a small pavilion goes up, open on every side, so nobody can say the other side hid archers. A low table. Tea already poured. A half moon in an empty sky. They meet the way they used to after sparring: gloves off, courtesy on.
[2] Bidam: Yushin. / Tea first. / …When the Six Elders raised Surabol — Lee, Choi, Jeong, Son, Bae, Seol. / Park came from an egg. / There was no Kim.
[3] Kim Yushin: …And?
[4] Bidam: And now the two Kim houses inside this wall — / Surabol Kim, Alji Kim — / both imports. / I alone… am Six-Elder blood.
[5] ¶ The tea cools between them. Neither man drinks enough to call it peace. Bidam smiles as if nothing ugly had been said — the same smile he wore when he crowned a woman king. Yushin sets his cup down unfinished.
[6] Bidam: Alchun sends his regards. From the middle of the field. / He’s eating alone again.
[7] Kim Yushin: He always did eat between us.
[8] ¶ Three Hwarang. One princess. The yard remembers what the Council never wrote down.
[9] ▼ FLASHBACK 615 The cleverest of the three
    [9.0] ¶ Bidam, Alchun, and Yushin — same Hwarang line, same bruised knuckles, same impossible orbit around **Princess Dukman**. They do not say the word love. The gyuku field says it for them, badly.
    [9.1] Bidam: If the Sacred Bone runs out of men, pick the cleverest woman. / I have known Dukman since we were children. Cleverness is not a gender.
    [9.2] Kim Yushin: Well stood. / Tomorrow on the yard — the hundred-and-ninth is mine.
    [9.3] Alchun: You two will kill each other over a score. / I will kill myself over the girl in the middle. / …That was a joke. File it as a joke.
    [9.4] Queen Sunduk: If you three are finished deciding my life— / the ball is still on the field.
    [9.5] ¶ Even their names take sides. Bidam’s sounds like this soil and its sutras. Chunchu’s is a foreign classic. Any clerk across the sea could file it without asking. Nobody notices yet. Names are patient.
    [9.6] Bidam: Yushin. / Alchun. / If either of you ever makes her cry for a small reason — I will even the score on your face.
[9] ▲ end flashback
[10] ══ DAY: DAY 3 ══
[11] ¶ Arrows trade; messengers lie; the Harmony Council discovers it can convene without deciding anything, which is its highest form. Chunchu’s clerks call the unanimity rule quaint. Bidam calls it ours. Inside the palace, the stewards count eight days of grain.
[12] [battle]
[13] ¶ **Third night.** Same pavilion. Same half moon. Bidam has brought a map — not of the siege, of the roads west.
[14] Bidam: Samhan is being colonized — in blood, and in the mind. / Tang sends institutions. India sends… / …through Queen Heo’s blood, sutras. / Yushin — your eyes are handsome. They are a western colour. / …When I stood first, they called me the liberal.
[15] Kim Yushin: Gaya blood came from the west too. / I… stood up. / Fifteen winters past, when you spoke — you told me to stand.
[16] Bidam: That was when you were weak. / …A joke. Drink your tea.
[17] ¶ On the wall Bidam looks west and remembers a cleaner war — Jade Gate Valley, when the enemy still had the courtesy to be foreign.
[18] ▼ FLASHBACK 636 Jade Gate Valley · 옥문곡
    [18.0] ¶ Baekje sends five hundred armoured men to slip through a valley in the dark and bite a fortress from behind. In midwinter the toads in the palace pond start croaking, which toads do not do. The queen listens for one night. Then she sends steel instead of prayers.
    [18.1] Alchun: Bidam — left ridge. I take the dry creek. / If their captain loosens a saddle, we do not wait for a committee.
    [18.2] Bidam: Finally — an enemy I am allowed to hate in public. / Alchun. On my mark.
    [18.3] ¶ They fall on the Baekje camp at dusk. Their captain climbs a boulder and empties a quiver; the quiver ends before the argument does. Alchun takes the general. Bidam takes the valley’s silence.
    [18.4] Alchun: We make a good pair when the target is outside the wall. / Inside the wall… we will see.
    [18.5] Bidam: Inside the wall is still the sacred country. / I do not miss.
    [18.6] ¶ Eleven years later, on Radiance’s rampart, Bidam will remember the Jade Gate as the last time Alchun stood on his side without hesitating.
[18] ▲ end flashback
[19] ¶ Before the fourth night’s tea, the Moon Palace tries a quieter weapon. Chunchu sends his son **Bupmin**, twenty-one, to the steam — the water that shows a man’s inner conscience, the past that is driving his hand. Yushin is told only to **keep him talking**.
[20] ¶ Chunchu is home from the islands. They kept him just long enough to be rude about it, then sent him back with compliments and no ships.
[21] King Muyeol: Bupmin. / Take a jar. / The spring is a place your uncle knows. You’re a Kim — the door will open. / Splash him.
[22] King Munmu: Father… / What does the water do to a man… / I understand. I’ll go.
[23] ── SCENE: The Steam Cavern ──
[24] ¶ This is the first time the cavern goddesses meet Bupmin. He is twenty-one. He does not yet have a king’s name. He has a jar and Chunchu’s weather.
[25] Narim: A Kim. / Sit. No — the jar first. / You… He is the best of both. Gaya in the shoulders. Surabol in the mouth. Golhwa is going to climb you if you stay standing. Sit.
[26] Golhwa: Oh. / A Kim we haven’t had. He’s both. / Take the water. Conscience sticks to it. Trauma. Grudge. Whatever’s driving the hand. / …And stop standing like that.
[27] Golhwa: I’m trying to be a hill and you are shaped like a problem I want in my lap.
[28] Hyullé: …Be careful. / If you splash it, you see why he’s doing it. / If you don’t see anything… that’s its own answer. / …He’s pretty. I’ll be quiet. I won’t be calm.
[29] King Munmu: Goddesses… / Thank you. I was only— / I’ll just take the water.
[30] ¶ He fills the jar. He does not stay for the lake’s other lessons. He is the best of both, and he leaves because his father told him to.
[31] ══ DAY: DAY 4 ══
[32] ¶ Seven days of grain. The Moon Palace’s wells drop. Rumour rises to replace them. Chunchu files contingency letters the way other men file prayers.
[33] ¶ Fourth night. Same low table under the half moon. Bidam reads a rumoured draft — never enough secretariat, never enough emperor. His voice stays pleasant. The sentences do not.
[34] Bidam: What Chunchu wants… / is a country that fits inside a Tang envelope. / Central rule. Emperor. Clerks. / He would burn the Harmony Council’s unanimity — the one thing we kept.
[35] Kim Yushin: Baekje comes with swords, not sentences.
[36] Bidam: Yes — and that is why you always win. / On the yard, and here. / Effort… speaks louder than my blood. / …The year they crowned her, I was the liberal who stood for the woman king. / Now they call me the blood-and-soil man. Ironic, Yushin?
[37] Kim Yushin: …That young Hwarang is still here.
[38] Bidam: Where?
[39] ¶ He folds the rumoured draft. The next sentences have been waiting in the sleeve all night.
[40] Bidam: Princess Seungman, and the tyranny of Kim Chunchu — I stand against both. / He speaks of a thousand-year kingdom. / If his faction wins, Samhan will spend those thousand years as a Chinese vassal. / A country that never again turns its own wheel.
[41] Kim Yushin: Under Seungman, with these reforms, Silla could be the strongest country in Samhan in a few harvests.
[42] Bidam: I do not need the strongest nation. / I want neighbours who still know one another’s names. / The young lifting the old. / A true people — not strangers who happen to share a wall.
[43] Kim Yushin: The people’s livelihood hangs on the nation’s fullness. / Fullness hangs on institutions — on a government that can still stand. / If Silla falls behind Baekje and Goryeo, what comes through the pass is spear and famine. / Then tell me how the neighbours keep their names.
[44] Bidam: Yushin. / Has the royal house spent one year outside the capital? Has Chunchu? / I have. / Out there, nobody wants a foreign emperor’s yoke.
[45] Kim Yushin: As for outsiders, Lord Bidam, I will always be more outsider than you. / You, of Six-Elder blood, speak poorly of the halls that raised this land, / while I, last son of a conquered kingdom, would die for it.
[46] ¶ Yushin does not close the argument. He asks again about the pass, about names, about harvests — anything that keeps Bidam’s back to the dark. Behind the pavilion, Bupmin’s jar ticks once against a post.
[47] Kim Yushin: Bidam. / Say it once more. / The people have no wish for an emperor. Where did you hear that?
[48] ¶ Bupmin comes from behind to **splash the water**. It is ugly and precise — cavern water as a hard sheet across Bidam’s shoulders, beads and all.
[49] Bidam: Ha… / What is this…
[50] King Munmu: Your trauma…. / Yushin… why isn’t it doing anything…?
[51] ¶ Nothing rises. No childhood. No princess. No grudge-film in the steam. The water runs off the black robe as if it had mistaken a man for a wound. Chunchu, at the pavilion’s edge, does not move. The stoic act holds; the eyes do not.
[52] King Muyeol: ……
[53] Bidam: Oh… haha… / I’ve heard of this… this is that water, isn’t it…?
[54] Bidam: HAHAHAHAHA!
[55] Bidam: Behold, the arrogance of the sacred bone class!! / You really thought I had to have some sort of personal trauma?? / That that was the reason I was doing all of this? / That I hated the princess? The queen? / That I hated you, Chunchu, or Yushin? / Have you ever… even for a SECOND… considered the POSSIBILITY… / that your ideas are simply terrible? / That they’ll lead this nation to ruin? / That ANY reasonable man would oppose them? / Or are you so ARROGANT to assume… that EVERYTHING you lot do is correct… / and that the ONLY reason for ANYONE to disagree… is because they were suffering some sort of mental disease? Because they were angry and bitter? / Ha… well, my friends, I’m afraid all you’ve done tonight is prove your point. / You’ve proven yourself to be unworthy of leading any country. / So please… my friends… step aside…!
[56] ¶ Alchun, arriving late with a lamp, goes pale. An officer asks whether to seize the jar. Nobody answers. Bidam is still laughing, and still alive, and the beads are still counting.
[57] ── SCENE: Chunchu’s Rooms ──
[58] King Muyeol: If Bidam wins, the Secretariat becomes a quaint hobby. / If Bidam loses, we still have a dying queen and a Tang-shaped hole in the west. / The man would burn a good idea for arriving in a Tang envelope. That is the whole platform — and it polls well. / Munhee — pack for either weather.
[59] Munhee: I already packed. / I packed the year the Queen was crowned. You only notice in sieges.
[60] ¶ Alchun eats alone between the camps. Both sides send him wine. He drinks neither. Surabol will later call it treason with better stationery.
[61] ══ DAY: DAY 5 ══
[62] ¶ Fifth night — the pavilion again. They sit on the floor, alone, the way they used to meet on the training ground. The tea is cold before anyone raises a blade. Six days of grain.
[63] Kim Yushin: Second Blade of Samhan — Bidam!! Lay down your arms and give your loyalty back to the Blue Moon!!
[64] ¶ For a breath they are only the old score again — one hundred and eight to one hundred and eight — two boys who never let the other keep a lead. Then Bidam speaks, and the yard is gone.
[65] ▼ FLASHBACK 618 One hundred and eight
    [65.0] ¶ The yard after rain. Two Hwarang, neither willing to leave the mud with the score uneven.
    [65.1] Bidam: One hundred and eight…! / Today I take the lead, Gaya!
    [65.2] Kim Yushin: One hundred and eight. / Get up, hyung. An uneven number does not sleep.
    [65.3] Bidam: Ha! / Afraid it will be written that Gaya blood lost to Silla blood?
    [65.4] Kim Yushin: Written or not. / Again.
    [65.5] Bidam: …And don’t call me hyung when you’re winning.
    [65.6] ¶ They end the evening even. They always do.
[65] ▲ end flashback
[66] Bidam: Yushin. / In this country the smartest people hate this country, / and the most patriotic people… are all stupid. / That’s Silla. / The country you’re trying to sell.
[67] Bidam: Yushin…. / And besides — you… / **you were never even of Silla…!**
[68] Bidam: Blood is inevitable.
[69] ¶ The tea has not been touched. He says it like a compliment that curdled — still the gentleman, still the black robe, still the voice that once shielded this same man from the yard.
[70] Kim Yushin: Lord Bidam… I remember we swore our lives to this together…
[71] Bidam: You never had a country of your own — selling this one must cost you nothing… / But we are different. We cannot be cut from this land… / Would you hand the country my ancestors built to an emperor…! / I am a son of the sacred country.
[72] Kim Yushin: Selling — I have sold nothing. / Lord Chunchu only asks that we learn Tang’s institutions. Baekje comes with swords, not sentences.
[73] Bidam: Chunchu — 春秋. The man is named after a Chinese book. / And you would let him write the sacred country’s tomorrow. / Learn another country’s institutions long enough — and one morning, the learning is all that is left.
[74] Bidam: I will raise the sacred country’s glory again, / I will return the sacred country’s future to its own people!
[75] ¶ Yushin does not answer the speech. He looks at the cold tea as if the answer were at the bottom of the cup.
[76] Bidam: Yumjong says your great-grandfather drove Geumgwan to Surabol in a cart. / Fine. Everyone knows the cart. / Nobody talks about the grandfather. What did he hand over, Yushin?
[77] Kim Yushin: Leave the dead in their rooms, Bidam.
[78] Bidam: No. / Five nights you’ve drunk my tea and told me nothing that was yours. / Give me one thing. Then call me a traitor.
[79] ¶ For a long time the only sound is the wind through the open pavilion. Yushin has not said this aloud in Surabol since he was fifteen.
[80] Kim Yushin: …Baekje has a name for one night on the Gwansan road. / Ask any soldier over the western hills. They call it the Severing.
[81] Bidam: The night their king lost his head. Everyone knows it. A slave held the knife.
[82] Kim Yushin: A slave held the knife. / A man in a Gaya cone helm sat their king on a camp stool and told him to sit. / …That was my grandfather.
[83] ¶ Bidam’s beads stop for the second time this winter.
[84] Bidam: …A Gaya prince broke the oldest peace in Samhan. / For us.
[85] Kim Yushin: For Silla. / And his grandson sits at your table and hears he was never of it.
[86] Bidam: …Drink your tea, Marshal.
[87] ¶ Neither of them drinks. Bidam does not ask the grandfather’s name, and Yushin does not offer it. Some names a family keeps in a box.
[88] ¶ **A cone helm, a king on a camp stool, and a name Yushin won’t say. Who was his grandfather…?**

#43 Muryuk  (562)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: daegaya · tone: elegiac legend
Logline: The youngest son in the cart surrenders Gaya on one condition, then spends his life riding for Silla. Even south.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ His name was Muryuk. He was the youngest of three sons in a cart, and the only one who looked back.
[1] [MAP 562: Five hundred years of iron, gone in thirty.]
[2] ¶ For five hundred years the people of Gaya lived by iron and by six eggs, and they enjoyed great peace. Then Silla came shopping.
[3] ── SCENE: The Surrender ──
[4] ¶ The lord of Geumgwan did the arithmetic first. Baekje to the west, Silla to the north, a river of iron and no army worth the name.
[5] ¶ The cart is slow. The road to Surabol is long enough for a boy to change his mind several times.
[6] The lord of Geumgwan: Face front, Muryuk. / Your brothers are facing front.
[7] Kim Muryuk: Somebody should remember what it looked like. / …The harbour. Before.
[8] The lord of Geumgwan: Then remember it quietly. Kings don’t like being reminded what they bought.
[9] ¶ He keeps looking back until the river bends out of sight.
[10] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 4, Silla Annals — King Beopheung, yr. 19 (532); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 86): The lord of Geumgwan, Kim Guhae, came with his queen and three sons, bringing the treasury and precious things of the country, and surrendered.❞
[11] [CARD Kim Muryuk: The youngest son in the cart. Gaya handed over its crown. It did not hand over him.]
[12] ¶ The king on the dais has bought harbours before. He has never bought one that talks back.
[13] Kim Muryuk: If we are to surrender, I have one condition… / Let my father’s sons live in Silla without shame…
[14] King Beopheung: And what do you mean by that?
[15] Kim Muryuk: In Silla… I know a man’s blood decides everything… / Sacred Bone, True Bone… I know it all… / If my descendants — the sons and daughters of Suro and Heo — can take a worthy place… / then I too am ready to give Silla my life…
[16] King Beopheung: Very well. Your descendants shall be raised as True Bones of Silla.
[17] King Beopheung: In return you ride for me. North, west. Wherever the border itches. / …Even south.
[18] Kim Muryuk: …Even south.
[19] ¶ Three generations later, his grandson will still be told he is not really one of them.
[20] Kim Muryuk: Your grace is boundless… Your Majesty…!
[21] ── SCENE: The Night Road ──
[22] ¶ Twenty-two years later he is a Silla governor in a Gaya helm, because nobody has managed to make him take it off. One night on the Gwansan road, the King of Baekje rides into his ditch.
[23] ¶ You have seen that night from the king’s side. From the cone’s side it is shorter. A man who once begged at a king’s feet sits another king on a camp stool and does not draw his sword. The slave does the rest.
[24] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1): His grandfather Muryeok was Commander of the Army of the Sinju Circuit; he once led troops that captured the king of Baekje and four of his generals and took more than ten thousand heads. His father Seohyun rose to the rank of Sopan, Governor-General of Daeyang Province and Pacifier of all the armies of Daeyang Province.❞
[25] ¶ Ten thousand heads, says the record, and makes him a hero. He goes home and does not eat for two days.
[26] ¶ Before that, the slave who did the cutting comes to his tent with the king’s knife, because nobody else will take it.
[27] Dodo: My lord. They said give it to the Gaya one. / …That’s you, isn’t it?
[28] Kim Muryuk: Keep it. / A knife that’s done that once shouldn’t go home to a man with sons.
[29] ── SCENE: The Last Gate ──
[30] ¶ Eight years after that, the Cloud King comes for what is left of Gaya. He brings a boy-general, Sadaham. He brings Muryuk.
[31] Sadaham: They said too young. / The gate didn’t.
[32] Mugwan: Don’t die first.
[33] Sadaham: Then keep up.
[34] ¶ The tall Gaya cone still fights. The men on Daegaya’s gate wear the same helm Muryuk does.
[35] Kim Muryuk: Those are my father’s helms. / Let me walk up first. Alone.
[36] Sadaham: They’ll shoot you.
[37] Kim Muryuk: Then keep the gate warm for me.
[38] ¶ He walks to the gate with his helm in his hand. Nobody on the wall knows what to do with a Gaya face under a Silla banner. By the time they decide, he is talking. Gaya has always listened to a good price.
[39] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 4, Silla Annals — King Jinheung, yr. 23 (562), 9th month; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 98): In the ninth month Gaya rebelled. The king ordered Isabu to punish them, with Sadaham as deputy. Isabu brought up the army, and they all surrendered at once.❞
[40] ¶ The boy took his prize anyway. After the city fell he opened the prize-cages and kept only Alcheon dirt. Take the land. Leave the people.
[41] Sadaham: Alcheon dirt. / That’s enough.
[42] ¶ Muryuk watches the cages open and says nothing. It is the first Silla habit he has ever liked.
[43] ── SCENE: The Name ──
[44] ¶ He grows old in Surabol with a True Bone seal and a Gaya accent he never loses. His son Seohyun is clever and polite, and keeps walking into things while looking at clouds.
[45] Kim Muryuk: Seohyun. When you have a son— / Don’t give him a Silla name to make them like him. They won’t. / Give him one that keeps faith.
[46] Kim Seohyun: Father, I’m not even— there isn’t even a girl, I—
[47] Kim Muryuk: There will be. You walk into walls looking at clouds. / Some girl will find that charming. One.
[48] ¶ Then he says a name nobody has been given yet.
[49] Kim Muryuk: Yushin…
[50] ══ DAY: DAY 6 ══
[51] ¶ On the sixth night there are two cups on the pavilion table. Bidam poured them himself. Last night he found out whose grandson he has been calling a Gaya ox.
[52] ¶ **Five days of grain. Two cups poured. Will the grandson of the cone helm come to tea…?**
